installation.note: tail is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: tail displays the last lines of files. It's essential for monitoring log files, viewing recent entries, and checking the end of large files. The -f option follows file changes in real-time, making it perfect for log monitoring.
when_to_use: Check last lines of large files

misconceptions.title: tail shows beginning of file
misconceptions.misconception: tail displays the start of files
misconceptions.reality: tail shows the END of files. Use head to see the beginning. tail is perfect for logs where recent entries are at the end.
misconceptions.tip: tail = end of file, head = beginning of file. tail is most useful for logs.

misconceptions.title: tail -f requires file to exist
misconceptions.misconception: tail -f only works on existing files
misconceptions.reality: tail -f can follow files that don't exist yet - it will wait and display content when file is created. Useful for monitoring new log files.
misconceptions.tip: tail -f works on non-existent files - it waits for file creation.

common_pitfalls.description: tail on binary files shows garbled output
common_pitfalls.solution: tail works best on text files. For binary files, use appropriate tools or hexdump.

common_pitfalls.description: tail -f runs continuously and doesn't stop
common_pitfalls.solution: Press Ctrl+C to stop tail -f. It runs until interrupted.

common_pitfalls.issue: Using -f instead of -F for rotating logs
common_pitfalls.description: tail -f stops following after log rotation
common_pitfalls.solution: Use tail -F for log files that rotate. -F reopens file after rotation.

best_practices: Use tail -f for real-time log monitoring
Use tail -F for log files that rotate
Use -n to specify number of lines (default is 10)
Combine with grep: tail -f log.txt | grep error
Use tail for large files instead of cat
Use tail for log files where recent entries matter most
performance_tips: tail is very fast - only reads end of file
tail -f has minimal overhead for log monitoring
Much faster than cat for large files (only reads last N lines)
Use tail instead of cat for log files

additional_notes.default_lines: Default shows last 10 lines. Use -n to change.

additional_notes.log_rotation: Use -F instead of -f for log files that rotate (common in production)

additional_notes.common_pattern: Very common pattern: tail -f /var/log/syslog for system monitoring, tail -f application.log for app logs
